newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu visits settlement in show of defiance.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu visits settlement in show of defiance.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu paid his first official visit to a Jewish settlement in the West Bank on Tuesday in a show of defiance to Palestinians opposed to his policy of expanding such outposts.
He and PLO officials, in comments made separately, warned each other over their approaches to the peace process, which has all but sputtered to a halt since Netanyahu took office in June.

Netanyahu chose Ariel, one of the most entrenched Jewish communities in the West Bank, for his high-profile tour, a day after the Palestinian Authority called for an immediate halt to all settlement activity.
Cheered by hundreds of schoolchildren in Ariel, the right-wing leader gave no ground to worldwide opposition to expanding settlements.

"Do you really expect that a government was elected that said it intended to maintain the communities in Judea and Samaria and that the prime minister would not visit those communities?" Netanyahu told reporters at the settlement where 13,000 Israelis live, using Hebrew names for the West Bank.
"What, you don't understand that there were elections in Israel? The Arab world doesn't understand that there were elections in Israel?...And why not develop communities here?"
Netanyahu, who opposes creation of a Palestinian state, has approved building thousands of new homes in the settlements.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat blasted Netanyahu's policies in comments in Palestinian-ruled Bethlehem in the West Bank.
"Netanyahu has to go back and read agreements concerning the settlements. It was agreed no new single settlement would be added, no expansion of existing settlements," Arafat said.

Settlements, where more than 130,000 Jews live amid nearly two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, were left for final status talks by an interim peace deal signed by Israel's previous government and the PLO in September 1993.

The PLO, which set up self-rule enclaves in parts of the areas under interim deals, views Jewish settlement in the lands Israel occupied in the 1967 Middle East war as a provocation. Final status talks have yet to resume under Netanyahu.
Israel's former government officially imposed a settlement building freeze, but constructed homes in areas it hoped to keep in a final peace deal.
Netanyahu, who won Israel's May elections, enraged Arabs by rescinding the freeze.
Israel and the PLO also traded barbs over their slow-moving talks on a long overdue Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron, where 400 Jews live amid 100,000 Arabs.
"We are warning the Israeli government...we are holding it fully responsible for the delay," Arafat adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters.
"We're not impressed by the threats but we are impressed with the fact that they don't want to conclude an agreement," Netanyahu said.

Israeli newspapers quoted government sources as saying an attempt on Sunday by Palestinians in Gaza to drive on a road which Israel placed off-limits to Arab traffic was a signal that Arafat might seek further violent confrontation with Israel.
Sixty Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in gunbattles in September after Israel opened an entrance to a tourist tunnel near Moslem sites in Jerusalem.

"I really would not recommend...to think that we will permit some sort of series of events like those after the opening of the tunnel and that we would stand aside and agree to conduct negotiations...under the threat of violence," Netanyahu said.
